articles.title: How to use the UUFinds spreadsheet to build a shortlist you can actually buy from
articles.description: Use the UUFinds spreadsheet to narrow a category, compare exact listings and keep a shortlist with prices, options and source links.

sections.heading: Start with a question the catalogue can answer
paragraphs: Imagine looking for a dark jacket with a hood and a zip. You find three promising product cards, send yourself screenshots and come back on Friday. One screenshot crops out the title. Another shows a grey jacket with the hood folded inside. You can remember which one you liked, but you cannot tell which seller or option it belonged to. The most valuable thing to save from a UUFinds spreadsheet is the route back to a particular listing. Once you have that, you can compare prices, photos and options again when you need them.

On UUFinds Grid the spreadsheet opens in your browser. Its category, search, sorting and page controls are useful even if you never make a separate file. If you like keeping notes, a few lines in your phone work well. Give each candidate its own entry and save the product link first. Add the detail that made you open it in the first place. “Two-way zip visible in the front photo” is easier to check later than “looks nice.”

sections.heading: Search by the detail a seller is likely to put in a title
paragraphs: Think about which part of your description the catalogue can match. A product title may include “jacket” and a model name while saying nothing about its hood. Start with a distinctive model or a short product term. Use the category control to narrow your results. Inspect the gallery for details that a title cannot reliably express. Typing every preference into one search can hide a suitable result whose seller described it in a different language or used a shorter name.

When a search is too broad, change one thing at a time. Start in jackets, try a model name, then compare the remaining results. If you know exactly which earlier result you wanted, open your saved link and check its source product ID. Catalogue addresses, marketplace listing numbers and the names printed on a garment serve different purposes. Preserve the complete link alongside the number so you can identify which service issued it. A page number makes a convenient browsing bookmark while you are looking through results, but new additions can move an existing product to a different page.

sections.heading: Decide what you want the sort order to reveal
paragraphs: Latest is useful when you have already gone through a category and want to review newer entries. Popular can give you a manageable place to begin in a category you have never explored. Price order is helpful if your first question is whether an option might fall within your item budget. Each order answers a different question. For the jacket example, start with the category, choose a sort, open a few distinct designs and stop as soon as you have enough candidates to compare. Reading another fifty cards will do little to settle whether the second jacket has a detachable hood.

For each candidate, open the detail page before recording its price. Where a seller supplies variants, a listing may cover multiple styles or sizes. Look for the price attached to your selection, record the currency and leave a space for any costs quoted later by the purchasing platform. Otherwise your list can accidentally compare one item's starting price with another item's selected price. If you switch the display currency, keep the same currency across the entries and record the day on which you made the comparison.

sections.heading: Read each gallery with one specific question in mind
paragraphs: Use the first pass through a listing to identify the product itself. Does the image show the right cut, fastening and pocket arrangement? For the hooded jacket, a rear view can establish whether a hood appears on the photographed design. A close-up of the collar might reveal the fastening you need to see. Record exactly what the image shows. If it only shows the hood folded down, leave “detachable” unresolved until you can see a zip, button arrangement or credible written description for that option.

Use a second pass to find conflicts between photos. A gallery can include several colorways, close-ups of a different option or a styled outfit with accessories. Look for a consistent feature across two views such as a zipper pull, seam position or contrast panel. Read the captions around warehouse QC photos separately from the seller's promotional images. A warehouse image might answer a useful question about one photographed piece. To apply that observation to your shortlist, you still need a credible connection to the same source listing and option.

sections.heading: Give similar-looking listings separate entries
paragraphs: Two sellers can use similar photographs; one seller can put several colorways under one listing. Split the decision into two parts. First, compare listing IDs. Second, record the chosen style or size within each listing. If the IDs match but your two screenshots show different colors, check the selector. If they differ, keep separate entries even when the titles and pictures look identical. A visual match gives you a reason to investigate, while the IDs give you a way to navigate back to each candidate.

A practical shortlist fits on a small screen. Each entry can contain six things: product link, source ID, selected option, displayed price and currency, strongest evidence, and the question you still need answered. One example might read “navy, medium; rear view shows an attached hood; need seller's chest measurement.” A second might read “charcoal, medium; size table available; check whether cuffs adjust.” These notes tell you what to do during the next visit. A ranking such as first, second and third tells you very little if prices or availability change.

sections.heading: Reopen the source before following a buying link
paragraphs: On the day you plan to buy, open the original listing from your note, then open your preferred buying platform. Compare the source ID, the seller's selected option and its thumbnail on both pages. A cross-platform link can land on the correct product with a default option already displayed. Choose your saved variant again where required and read back the selected values before continuing. A translated color name can change between services. A seller's original option code, style thumbnail or SKU can help you resolve that difference.

Compare the amounts at the same stage of the purchase. If one page lists only the item and another includes a domestic delivery charge, write down both components before making a decision. If international delivery has not yet been quoted, keep it as an open cost in your notes. Review the buying platform's current terms for any question that affects whether you are willing to order. A price displayed during discovery is a reference you can check against the destination page when you choose the exact option.

sections.heading: Keep the shortlist useful after the first visit
paragraphs: When a saved listing disappears or a particular size is unavailable, keep its ID and the evidence you already collected. Mark the entry unavailable with the date you checked. Use the most distinctive details from it to restart your search. In the jacket example those might be a double zip and a concealed hood. An image search can surface possible replacements, but give each replacement a fresh entry and repeat the source and option checks. A substitute needs its own supporting photos and measurements.

When you share the finished list, send links with your reasoning in ordinary language. A friend who reads “the first jacket has the hood I wanted; the second is my backup if the seller confirms the measurements” can help you resolve the question. A friend who receives a gallery of cropped pictures has to reconstruct your work. Taking a few seconds to attach a link, an option and one observation to each find turns a browsing session into a decision you can pick up where you left off.

articles.title: UUFinds sneaker finds: matching the colorway, size label and seller SKU
articles.description: Choose the right seller colorway and size label, interpret foot-length charts and carry your sneaker SKU through to the buying platform.

sections.heading: Identify the pair you saw in the first photo
paragraphs: A sneaker card can show a white shoe with a blue heel while the listing opens on an entirely black pair. Multi-colorway listings put several shoes under the same product title. On the Oopbuy Lists Air Force 1 example, a single Weidian product ID sits above separate sections for product photos, styles and QC photos. That structure explains why two people can share the same product link and still have different shoes in mind. Before talking about size, identify the exact option that shows the pair you want.

Choose two landmarks that are clear in the image you started with. Try the color of the heel tab together with the shape of an overlay near the toe. Side stripes alone can be hard to distinguish when two adjacent styles share the same upper. Open the style selector and compare one candidate at a time against your landmarks. Save the seller's written style code or color description exactly as displayed. “Blue heel, grey outsole, option B” will survive a screen change much better than “fourth thumbnail from the left.”

sections.heading: Read the entire size label before choosing a number
paragraphs: A shoe size has a system and sometimes a wearer category. “8” alone is incomplete. Look for labels such as US men's, US women's, UK or EU, and preserve the text alongside the number. Brand charts can give separate rows for these systems. Nike's men's footwear chart, for example, displays US men's and US women's equivalents in separate rows and also identifies foot length. An EU number in a marketplace selector does not establish that the seller used a particular manufacturer's conversion table.

Read any marks attached to the number. A letter might identify a width, a youth category, or some other seller-specific distinction. Keep half sizes and fractions intact when copying your choice. A translation can remove punctuation or make a short option look simpler than the original. If the listing offers two entries with the same number and different suffixes, compare their original names and ask the seller what they mean if the pictures leave it unclear. It is better to resolve the duplicate labels now than to guess after placing an order.

sections.heading: Build a measurement you can use for comparison
paragraphs: If you do not know your foot length, start with the measuring directions accompanying the chart you plan to use. For its footwear guide Nike describes standing on paper on a firm surface, marking the ends of the foot and measuring the distance. Repeat for the other foot and use the longer measurement with that chart. Write down the unit and whether you measured with socks. You now have one reproducible piece of information for evaluating the listing and for explaining your question to a seller.

Pay attention to the heading above a number in centimeters. Nike distinguishes the CM size printed on a box or shoe label from measured foot length. An insole measurement is another separate value. Its endpoints and curved shape can produce a number different from the length of the foot that fits inside the shoe. If your own note says “26 cm,” expand it to “foot length, heel to longest toe” or “removable insole, measured flat” as appropriate. That small edit prevents you from looking up a number in the wrong row.

sections.heading: Find the chart for the model and the seller's size range
paragraphs: Check the product description and gallery for a chart that applies to the model or style you selected. Read its column headings, its units and any instructions about how the measurement was taken. If you are using a chart supplied by a brand, make sure it covers the intended footwear category. A chart for children's sizes or a table for a different model family can suggest an option that happens to have the same printed number. Keep the chart link or a screenshot with the headings visible.

A pair you already wear can provide a second reference. Record its model, full size label, width if stated and the aspect of its fit that works for you. “Room through the forefoot with my everyday socks” is more informative than “fits perfectly.” Use that reference to frame a question about the prospective pair. Does the seller have a width option? Can they identify the chart used for this style? A favorite pair can help you describe your needs without requiring every other shoe carrying the same number to fit the same way.

sections.heading: Select the style and size together
paragraphs: Choose the colorway first, then choose the size within that colorway and reread both values. If the listing disables a size after you change the style, that combination needs another check. Go back to your preferred colorway and confirm which sizes are currently selectable. Changing a single field can leave you looking at a valid combination for a different shoe. Look at the selected-option line, thumbnail and price together before you copy the link or move to another platform.

Save the source ID and SKU in separate fields whenever a SKU is available. The source ID identifies the listing. A SKU can distinguish one complete style and size combination within it. If the page only exposes a link to the whole item, save the exact seller labels as well. Sharing a URL along with “style B, EU 42, regular width” gives another person a way to check the choice even if their page opens with the first thumbnail selected. These are example labels, so substitute the actual wording on your listing.

sections.heading: Use the right picture to resolve a remaining doubt
paragraphs: Suppose two style thumbnails both look off-white. Compare the outsole edge, heel patch and the placement of colored stitching across multiple images. Different lighting can shift a pale upper toward grey or cream. A repeated detail visible from two camera angles is more useful for identifying the colorway than a single bright patch. If the style code is readable in an image, check it against the option label. A seller's code is particularly useful when two translated descriptions both become “white.”

For a size question, ask for a picture that answers it directly. A clear label photo can establish the printed system and size of the photographed pair. A measurement photo can show the span between two visible endpoints if the ruler and shoe are aligned. A side view or a photo of the box is much less useful for judging interior space. Add any unresolved issue to your notes before continuing. If the only photo belongs to a different style or size, describe it as a reference and ask about the actual combination.

sections.heading: Carry the selection through to the buying platform
paragraphs: When you open the destination product page, match the marketplace ID first. Then compare the selected colorway, size system, width and SKU against your saved entry. If the platform displays translated labels, use the original style code and thumbnail to connect the two views. If a copied option link lands on the default selection, select the combination manually. Read the price after making that choice and check whether the item is available in the quantity you want before adding it to an order.

One last check is especially helpful when you have compared several pairs in separate tabs. Read your choice as a single line: model, colorway, size system and size, width if supplied, seller option and source ID. Then read the corresponding fields on the destination page in the same order. You can usually spot a swapped color or a change from US men's to US women's immediately. Once those fields agree, save the final selection with your notes. If they disagree, return to the listing that supplied the original information and resolve that one difference before proceeding.

articles.title: UUFinds image search: find a product from a screenshot
articles.description: Search the UUFinds Grid catalogue with a photo, compare candidates across style and gallery images, and verify the seller and selected option before buying.

sections.heading: Start with a photo you can recognise again
paragraphs: Imagine someone sends you a photograph of a green shoulder bag. The caption has disappeared, and searching for “green bag” turns up everything from laptop sleeves to evening bags. Before you open image search, look at what you would actually recognise in another photograph. Perhaps the strap fastens to a silver ring below the zip, the corners curve inward, and the front has one vertical seam. Those three observations give you a way to judge the results even when every seller uses a different title.

On UUFinds Grid, the camera beside the catalogue search opens the image-search page. Choose a file showing the item. The comparison runs on your device against the indexed catalogue images, which include product, gallery and style photographs. An uploaded picture can therefore resemble an angle or colour shown inside a listing, even when its cover looks quite different. The result opens a catalogue product page. Keep the original photograph handy as you work through the candidates.

sections.heading: Choose a crop that answers your question
paragraphs: For a full product search, leave enough space around the item to show its outline. A close-up of the silver ring might be excellent for comparing hardware after you find the bag, yet dozens of different bags share that ring. Try an image that includes the handle, body and base. A little background is fine. Removing a coat sleeve, a retail price graphic or the much larger bag beside it usually makes the intended object clearer.

On a phone, duplicate the photograph in your photo editor before cropping. For a screenshot of a shopping page, start the crop below the navigation bar and end it above the row of suggested products. A screenshot showing four colour options needs a separate crop for the particular colour you want. Keep the other version in case the chosen square is too small to show the shape. Stretching a thumbnail or sharpening it aggressively can give its edges a different appearance without recovering missing detail.

Sometimes a detail is the entire question. For example, you may already recognise a jacket but need to find the colourway with a contrasting lower pocket. Make one crop of the whole jacket and one that includes the pocket and enough surrounding fabric to show where it sits. Run the searches separately. If both lead to the same listing, open its style selector and look for that colourway. A repeat appearance gives you a candidate worth inspecting.

sections.heading: Read a results page from the pictures inward
paragraphs: Look through several images before reading their translated titles. With the green bag, a front view can make a tote look like the one in the screenshot while a side view reveals a deep, boxy base. Open the candidate with the correct attachment and the candidate with the correct silhouette in separate tabs. Write down which feature each one explains. A seller can show a dark green sample against a white wall and a light green one against grey. Colour alone makes a weak tie-breaker.

On the product page, look for the particular photo that led to the match. A gallery may contain packaging, a model wearing the item or a whole group of products. If a matched image shows five bags together, inspect the selectable styles to see whether the pictured shape is actually offered. For clothing, useful landmarks include the position of a chest pocket relative to a seam and the shape of the cuff. For footwear, compare the sole edge, heel construction and lace layout across more than one angle.

sections.heading: Follow the match back to its source
paragraphs: Once one candidate explains the distinctive details, open its original listing and record the marketplace and product ID. If you later compare an agent page, check the original listing attached to it. A product ID is a much more convenient bookmark than “third green bag on the results page.” It also lets another person return to the item after the search order changes or after the seller changes the cover photograph.

The product page can group several options under one number. In our bag example, one option might show the right pocket and a short handle while another includes the longer shoulder strap in your screenshot. Select each relevant option and inspect the image that appears. Record the seller’s option label alongside the item number, including capital letters or numbers in the style code. Keep a screenshot of your selection if the name is translated differently on the next platform.

If the candidate has QC photos, read the caption and check whether an option is identified. A seller gallery can help answer “does this listing show the bag I recognise?” A warehouse image tied to a particular selection can help answer “what details were visible on that photographed item?” If no option is shown, you can still inspect the seam or fastener in the frame, but leave the colourway attribution open. This is particularly important when several candidates use the same polished studio photograph.

sections.heading: Diagnose a disappointing result
paragraphs: If the page returns a row of unrelated black rectangles after you submit a black wallet, inspect your own image at thumbnail size. Does the white price sticker occupy a third of it? Does the wallet merge into a dark table? Try a second photo with the wallet open or turn to a view showing its outline. Change one thing at a time so you can tell whether the better result came from the angle, the crop or the background.

A nearly identical image belonging to a different seller calls for a different decision. Another crop of exactly the same studio shot may keep finding the same photograph. Use the original post to look for a store name, an order link or a model code. Search the spreadsheet with the most distinctive text you can actually read. If you can recover a marketplace link from the sender, use that link as the starting point for the next lookup. It gives you a seller and listing to verify independently of the image.

An empty result after the comparison finishes and a message that the catalogue could not load are different situations. For the former, try a simpler image or switch to text search. For the latter, retry when the page can load its search data. If the device rejects a file, export a smaller JPEG or PNG and select it again. There is little value in repeatedly submitting a screenshot that still includes the entire browser window or the wrong item.

sections.heading: Save a useful record of the find
paragraphs: For a useful handoff, write a short sentence about the match and keep the original product address with it. For example, “Green shoulder bag, front seam below clasp, long-strap option shown in second gallery image” tells a friend what to look for. Add the marketplace, item ID and selected style code once you have confirmed them. If two candidates remain, save both addresses and name the one detail that would decide between them. That is easier to revisit than a stack of apparently identical screenshots.

Finish the search when you can explain why you chose the listing and identify what the photos leave unresolved. If the seller’s page shows the right bag from the front but never shows the strap attachment, ask for a photograph of that attachment if it matters to your choice. If you simply wanted a similar shape, the closest suitable alternative may be enough. Either way, the result of a visual search becomes useful when it leads to a product page and a selection you can describe.

articles.title: Weidian, Taobao and 1688 links: find the right item ID for a UUFinds lookup
articles.description: Identify a Weidian item ID, Taobao listing ID or 1688 offer number, recover the source link and keep a selected SKU attached to the right product.

sections.heading: Find the page that describes one item
paragraphs: A message arrives with a product photo, a share link and a note saying “the brown pair in size 40.” You open the link and see a shop with twenty pairs of boots. The photograph has given you a lead, but the shop address sends the next person to the same twenty choices. Open the individual pair and make sure that the page has its own product title and options. Then copy the product address. Starting here saves an awkward round of messages about which pair you meant.

When you use UUFinds, the type of address matters. Its developer’s Chrome Web Store description identifies Weidian, Taobao, 1688 and agent links as inputs for its link-conversion workflow. On this independent UUFinds Grid site, the spreadsheet searches its own catalogue; the product page provides a route to the original listing. A successful lookup on one service does not establish that the other has the same item or any warehouse photographs. Keep the original address until you have finished comparing the results.

sections.heading: Recognise the three common address formats
paragraphs: In a typical Weidian desktop item address, read the value of the itemID field. The listing used for the Grid example has the address https://weidian.com/item.html?itemID=7880141682. The source number is 7880141682. A detail page elsewhere may include other numbers in its path or in the selected options. Compare those against the actual field in the original address before you call one of them the item ID. Keep the field name with the number when explaining it to someone else.

A common Taobao desktop address uses the host item.taobao.com, the path /item.htm and a field called id. You may see other fields after an ampersand. Read the number belonging to id and save the complete address you opened. On a common 1688 desktop offer page, the number appears inside the path on detail.1688.com, between /offer/ and .html. The QCDock link checker publishes examples for both formats; they are useful if you need to see where a number sits in an actual product address.

Phone share links can look different from these desktop examples. A recognisable domain and a plausible number make a starting point, but the title, seller and item options are still worth checking. Keep numbers as text when saving them to a spreadsheet. A column formatted as a number may display a long ID in scientific notation, making it hard to read back over a call. If the number you received is already rounded, go back to the original address before copying it into a new link.

sections.heading: Keep the catalogue row, listing and SKU together
paragraphs: The UUFinds Grid example shows why two people can quote different numbers and both be looking at the same product. The English catalogue page ends in /en/shoes/3475.html. Here 3475 belongs to the catalogue address. The page identifies 7880141682 as the source product, which matches the Weidian itemID field. Use the Grid address to return to its layout and language, and the marketplace address to locate the seller’s listing. Those two numbers have different jobs.

Now choose a specific style and size. The seller may assign a SKU to that combination. A product with a dozen styles can have one listing ID and many combinations that share it. When sending an option to a buyer, include the original marketplace URL, the style exactly as displayed and the size label. Add the SKU if the selected combination exposes one. If a link opens on the default colour on another device, the written option gives the recipient a way to select it again.

This distinction also helps when comparing prices. A result may show a reference price before you choose anything, and a selected combination can have a different price. Write down which option you selected, the currency you saw and whether the amount covered one item or a bundle. Two pages can resolve to the same seller listing yet show different values because their initial selections differ. Confirm the final choice on the buying platform before you treat either amount as your order total.

sections.heading: Open short and agent links without losing the original
paragraphs: A short share link may consist of a short host name and a few letters. Follow it in your usual browser and inspect where it lands. If it opens an app, use the share control on the individual product rather than copying the store’s home page. When someone sends a paragraph of promotional text with several links, ask which one opens the item shown. A coupon, shop invitation and product listing can all appear in a single shared message.

An agent page sometimes offers an original-listing button. That is a convenient place to recover the marketplace address. Other pages embed an address after a field such as url. If the embedded text contains percent signs, preserving the entire agent link is safer than manually deleting chunks until something looks like a URL. Open the agent page, use its original listing option when available and compare the seller and item on arrival. If the agent obscures the original address, label the source as unresolved rather than attaching an ID from a similar photograph.

For a shared spreadsheet, give the original and agent links separate columns. If a colleague prefers a different agent, you can send the same marketplace item without asking them to reconstruct its identity from the current agent’s URL. Keep a third column for the option. That helps when one person likes the bag in the hero image and another wants the smaller size shown halfway down the gallery. Both can be referring to the same product number.

sections.heading: Interpret a missing lookup result
paragraphs: First test the original item page. If it opens and still describes the expected product, check what you pasted into the lookup. A shop number, a SKU or a catalogue row number may produce an empty result where the item ID works. Try the full marketplace link on a service that documents support for it. On the Grid spreadsheet, also try a distinctive model or part of the product title. Check any result against the source number on its detail page.

If you find a matching product but no QC images, you have answered the identity question. You can retain the useful listing while leaving photo coverage as an open question. A visually similar item from another shop can offer a comparison of general shape. Its pictures do not document a particular purchase from the seller whose number you recorded. If the link reaches a removed listing, save the address and ask the sender or seller whether there is a replacement. A newly published listing may carry a new number even when the product name looks familiar.

sections.heading: Hand over a link another person can verify
paragraphs: A short handoff can cover almost everything that matters. For the worked example, include “Weidian item 7880141682,” its original address, the Grid page if you used it, and the exact style and size you intend to buy. Ask the recipient to open the source and tell you which selection is highlighted. If the answer differs from yours, compare the written option labels while you both have the product open. It takes less work to resolve a mismatched colour at that stage than after an order has been placed.

For items that remain candidates, note what you still need. “Same listing, available size unknown” is more informative than an unqualified tick in a spreadsheet. “Same photo, seller unconfirmed” gives the next researcher a clear reason to request the original link. The aim is a record that survives a language change, a new agent or a rewritten listing title. A marketplace name, a source number and a clearly documented option do most of that work.
